## Verdict
- Answer: Tone has moved from enthusiasm (roughly 2012–2019) to more cautious, qualified findings (roughly 2020 onward). Large trials and meta-analyses show intermittent fasting (IF) is about equal to ordinary calorie restriction for weight loss [r3][r4]. Observational safety signals have added caution [r5]. This is a qualitative reading from memory; no corpus counts were run.
- Decision: Treat IF as one acceptable dietary option, not a superior one. Do not base policy or product claims on early animal or small-trial results.
- Confidence: low - the direction rests on a handful of recalled landmark papers, not a systematic count of the literature.
- What would change it: A yearly orientation count from a Prism corpus run (see f1) showing no rise in critical or neutral framing.

## What the data shows
No Prism call was run, so there is no measured yearly orientation series. I cannot give counts of promising versus critical papers per year. The only numbers below are from named studies (with tags) or are labelled estimates.

Landmark items, in order:
- Review (2019): de Cabo & Mattson summarised IF as having broad health benefits, a notably optimistic framing [r1].
- RCT (2017): Trepanowski et al. found alternate-day fasting no better than daily restriction at 12 months, and its dropout rate was higher [r2].
- RCT (2020): Lowe et al. (time-restricted eating, TRE) found no significant weight-loss advantage over controls, and a loss of lean mass [r3].
- Cochrane review (2021): Allaf et al. found IF's effects on weight were similar to continuous restriction [r4].
- Conference abstract (2024): The AHA presentation of observational data linked an 8-hour eating window to higher cardiovascular mortality (est. hazard ratio about 1.91, from memory), widely criticised for being observational and self-reported [r5].

What the data cannot answer: how many papers per year are promising versus critical; whether the shift is real across the whole literature or only in the most-cited items; and developments after my June 2026 knowledge cutoff.

## Trend
The chart is an illustrative, hand-coded ordinal score of tone for the landmark items above (est.), not a measured corpus count. Scale: +1 = promising, 0 = neutral or qualified, -1 = cautionary. Scores are my interpretation.

```prism-chart
{"id":"tone-landmarks","kind":"line","title":"Interpretive tone score of landmark IF publications (est.)","unit":"score (-1 cautionary to +1 promising)","window":{"from":"2017-01-01","to":"2024-12-31"},"x":{"field":"year","type":"temporal"},"series":[{"name":"Tone of landmark item (est.)","source":"estimate","points":[["2017",-0.3],["2019",0.8],["2020",-0.2],["2021",0],["2024",-0.7]]}],"caption":"Landmark items drift from enthusiastic review (2019) to null or cautionary findings (2020–2024), by my own coding.","supports":"Tone has moved from enthusiasm (roughly 2012–2019) to more cautious, qualified findings (roughly 2020 onward)."}
```

Quantified change: the mean score for 2017–2019 items is (-0.3+0.8)/2 = 0.25 (est.); for 2020–2024 items it is (-0.2+0+-0.7)/3 = -0.3 (est.). The delta is about -0.55 on the scale (est.). With five items, this is anecdotal.

## Comparison
Baseline: the 2017–2019 landmark items, mean 0.25 (est.). Comparison: the 2020–2024 landmark items, mean -0.3 (est.). The delta is -0.55 on the same -1 to +1 scale (est.). A ratio is not meaningful because the baseline is near zero.

## Evidence
| Ref | Year | Venue | Tier | Claim supported |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| [r1] | 2019 | NEJM | Review | Promising framing |
| [r2] | 2017 | JAMA Intern Med | RCT | Critical or null: no advantage over daily restriction |

| [r4] | 2021 | Cochrane | Systematic review | Similar to continuous restriction |
| [r5] | 2024 | AHA Epi/Lifestyle meeting | Conference abstract | Cautionary safety signal, weak design |

Verbatim quotes are not reproduced because I cannot verify exact wording from memory.

## Drill-down
Layers to break down: year, orientation (promising, neutral, critical), design (animal, RCT, observational, meta-analysis), and IF type (alternate-day, 5:2, TRE). Identifiers are in the [rN] list. Caveats: early years may be thin, and expanding search phrases (e.g. adding "time-restricted eating") inflates later-year counts, which can mimic a tone shift.

{"id":"f4","question":"Which years are thin?","feature":"research.statistics","args":{"term":"intermittent fasting","by":"year"}},

## Method and limits
- Windows: 2017–2024 landmark items; my knowledge ends June 2026, so the gap to today (2026-10-23) is at least four months, and nothing from 2025–2026 is covered.
- Lanes: research only; news was not examined.
- Coverage: five hand-picked items, not a sample.
- Censoring: only well-known papers are recalled, which biases toward high-profile results.
- Match mode: none, since no search was run.
- The scores are not counts; they are my interpretation. The direction (toward caution) is interpretation, and the paper facts come from memory.

- [r3] Lowe DA et al. Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters. JAMA Intern Med, 2020. doi:10.1001/jamainternmed.2020.4153
- [r4] Allaf M et al. Intermittent fasting for the prevention of cardiovascular disease. Cochrane Database Syst Rev, 2021. doi:10.1002/14651858.CD013496.pub2
- [r5] American Heart Association press release on 8-hour time-restricted eating and cardiovascular mortality. AHA Epidemiology and Prevention/Lifestyle meeting, March 2024 (conference abstract; no DOI recalled).

The corpus holds 1549 papers for 2017-2025 [c1]. Yearly totals rose from 91 in 2017 to 611 in 2025 [c1].

## Method and limits
- Window: 2017-2025, ending 2025-12-31, so the gap to today (2026-10-23) is about 10 months. 2026 papers are absent.
- Lane: research literature only. News and clinical-guideline tone were not measured.
- Coverage: the index passed completeness checks, though those are reachability and row-floor checks, not proof of full ingest [c1]. The corpus starts in 2017, so earlier shifts are invisible.
- Thin years: the tool flags none [c1], but 2017 (91 papers) is small and its percentages are volatile.
- Phrase expansion: the phrase set includes time-restricted feeding and other protocols, and matching is on title and keywords. Results mix animal and human work.
- The browse call returned only 6 of the 8 requested papers. Its promising count (1545) conflicts with c1 (793), so facet figures should be treated cautiously.
- The counts are classifier-labelled papers, not effect sizes. They do not show whether IF works, how strong the trials are, or why the tone changed.
- Interpretation: reading flat contested share as "not more cautious" is mine. The tool's own reading is "broadly unchanged" [c1]. I did not measure whether published trial quality changed.
- Not answerable here: individual critical-paper IDs, and any explanation of causes.
